Machpelah
mak-PEE-lah
proper noun (the patriarchs' burial cave)
Hebrew Makpelah, perhaps “double” (a double cave); the field and cave near Hebron that Abraham bought to bury Sarah, the burying-place of the patriarchs.

Biblical Definition

Machpelah was the field and cave near Mamre, in Hebron in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a burying-place for Sarah—the first piece of the promised land that the patriarch possessed. Though God had promised him the whole land, Abraham owned none of it in his lifetime save this grave; he insisted on buying it at full price, refusing it as a gift, that it might be a secure and lawful possession. There Sarah was buried, and afterward Abraham himself, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah, and at last Jacob, whose dying charge was that his sons carry his body up out of Egypt to lay him in the cave of Machpelah with his fathers. The dictionary marks Machpelah for its quiet but profound testimony of faith. Abraham's purchase of a grave in Canaan was an act of faith in the promise: he buried his dead in the land God had sworn to give his seed, declaring by that very act his confidence that the promise would stand though he himself died a stranger and pilgrim. So the writer to the Hebrews says of the patriarchs that they all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Machpelah is the grave of pilgrims who looked for a better country—men who held the earthly land as the pledge of a heavenly inheritance, and who, dying in faith, were buried in hope of the resurrection and the city whose builder and maker is God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The field and cave near Hebron that Abraham bought to bury Sarah, the burying-place of the patriarchs (Genesis 23:9-19); the one piece of the promised land Abraham owned, and a testimony of faith—pilgrims buried in hope of the promise.

MACHPELAH, proper noun. [Hebrew Makpelah, perhaps “double.”] The patriarchs' burial cave near Hebron.

Abraham bought it from Ephron the Hittite to bury Sarah (Genesis 23:9).

The one piece of the promised land Abraham possessed in his lifetime.

There were buried Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob (Genesis 49:30-31).

A testimony of faith: pilgrims buried in hope of the promise (Hebrews 11:13).

Key Scripture

Ge 23:9 — "That he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field; for as much money as it is worth he shall give it me for a possession of a buryingplace amongst you."

Ge 23:19 — "And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan."

Ge 49:30 — "In the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, which is before Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field of Ephron the Hittite for a possession of a buryingplace."

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is reading Machpelah as mere ancient real estate, missing the testimony of faith—a grave bought as a pledge of the promise.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faith that buried its dead in the land of promise. A merely historical reading treats Machpelah as a property transaction—an old man buying a grave. Scripture frames it as an act of faith. God had promised Abraham the whole land, yet he owned none of it in his lifetime save this cave; and he insisted on buying it at full price, refusing it as a gift, that he might possess in Canaan a lawful pledge of the promise. To bury Sarah in the promised land was to confess that the promise would stand though he died a stranger in it.

So the patriarchs were laid one by one in Machpelah—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives—and Jacob's dying charge to be carried up out of Egypt to that cave was a last confession of faith in the land God had sworn. The writer to the Hebrews gives the meaning: they all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off and embraced them, confessing themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth, looking for a better country. The dictionary holds Machpelah as the grave of pilgrims who held the earthly land as the pledge of a heavenly inheritance, and who died in hope of the resurrection and the city whose builder and maker is God.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew Makpelah (perhaps “double,” a double cave); the field and cave near Mamre at Hebron, Abraham's purchased burying-place for the patriarchs.

Makpelah, Hebrew, perhaps “double” (a double cave).

The field and cave “before Mamre,” that is, Hebron, in Canaan.

Bought by Abraham from Ephron the Hittite at full price (Genesis 23:9).

The one possession of the promised land Abraham held in his lifetime.

The burying-place of Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob.

Usage

"The teacher preached Machpelah as Abraham's act of faith—a grave bought as a pledge of the promise."

"He noted the patriarchs all died in faith, buried as strangers and pilgrims in the land God swore."

"She saw in the patriarchs' tomb the hope of resurrection and the city whose builder is God."
